item.title: Personable — Relationships and Well-being
item.description:
AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
Nicolò Pagan et al.
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 20 October 2026

Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

Extra-Familial Intergenerational Contact in the Contemporary United States: Exploring Its Frequency, Nature, and Correlates
Craig Fowler & Jessica Gasiorek
Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, forthcoming

Abstract:
Some major studies conducted over the last forty years suggest that intergenerational contact between younger and older adults (i.e., those aged 70+) in Western contexts is scarce. However, the phrasing of questions asked in these studies leaves open the possibility that intergenerational contact might not be so rare. In Study 1 (n = 399), we surveyed young Americans about the frequency and characteristics of their intergenerational interactions. In Study 2 (n = 278), we surveyed a separate sample of young Americans to assess the quantity and communicative quality of their contact with older people, gather information about their intergenerational relationships, and gauge their attitudes towards aging. In Study 1, 42% of respondents had at least one friend aged 70 or older and over 60% had had contact (typically face-to-face) with an older adult during the previous week. In Study 2, the quality and quantity of contact were associated with the endorsement of prescriptive age-based stereotypes, both directly and indirectly via perceptions of common ingroup identity. Moreover, quantity and quality of contact predicted the affective responses younger adults had at the thought of growing old, and their sense of efficacy about doing so. Our results suggest that the state of intergenerational relations in the United States is less dire than some might believe, and that high-quality contact with older adults is associated not only with less negative stereotypes but also younger people feeling both less troubled by and better able to cope with their own aging.

Gender and Interracial Relationship Dissolution: Evidence from a Decade of Roommate Outcomes
Catherine Shea et al.
Social Psychology Quarterly, forthcoming

Abstract:
Using a natural experiment at an elite college (1982–1991), we analyze roommate choices following random first-year assignments, during a period when the Asian-student population doubled. This design allows us to test how shifting demographics affect interracial tie dissolution. Focusing on white-Asian dyads, we find a significant gender divide: Women exhibit consistently high rates of interracial relationship dissolution regardless of population composition, whereas men's interracial ties are affected by population shifts, with tie dissolution increasing as minorities have more same-race outside options. These findings shift the study of intergroup contact from relationship formation to durability, demonstrating that opportunity structures shape interracial relationship dissolution in a setting largely free from self-selection processes that characterize most naturally occurring ties.

The Pain of Ghosting? People Underestimate How Bad Their Conversation Partners Feel About Not Responding
Sophia Li, Coral Zheng & Juliana Schroeder
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
Although online communication platforms provide convenience, they also bring a risk of ghosting, when one person unexpectedly stops responding to another without explanation. Extending prior research that examines the pain of being ghosted, we instead examine whether the act of ghosting itself is emotionally painful -- and whether people recognize the extent of ghosters’ bad feelings. Across three studies -- recalled real ghosting experiences (N = 195), imagined ghosting scenarios (N = 601), and induced ghosting in a live interaction (N = 350) -- we find that people who are ghosted underestimate how bad their conversation partners feel about ghosting them. This underestimation is larger when the ghosting is unintentional and mitigated when communicators do not perceive their actions as ghosting or send a short response (e.g., “sorry, can’t talk”) instead of ghosting. Overall, this research provides a window into the overlooked pain of ghosting others.

More Than a Song: Collective Singing Increases Well-being and Self-Expansion Via Collective Effervescence
Shira Gabriel et al.
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
Humans have been singing with other humans across time and culture. Although past research found positive effects of singing with others, it has not disentangled those effects from being in an established collective. In the current research, we examined the hypothesis that singing in groups leads to increased feelings of well-being and self-expansion even without an established collective. Furthermore, we hypothesized that the main mechanism for these effects is a feeling of collective effervescence -- an intertwining sense that one is connected to others and that something special is happening. Finally, we hypothesized that the positive effects of collective effervescence felt during a singing event can last weeks, even months, after the event. Across two experiments and a longitudinal study, we found support for our hypotheses. Singing in groups predicts positive outcomes (e.g., positive mood, satisfaction with life, self-concept change, donation intentions), primarily via the collective effervescence experienced at these events.

item.title: What a Deal — Products and Consumers
item.description:
The Humanizing Power of Accents in Voicebots: When Accent-Based Humanization Increases User Engagement
Hesam Ghasemi, Amir Sepehri & Cait Lamberton
Journal of Marketing Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Given that consumers often exhibit resistance toward algorithmic systems, firms face challenges in encouraging engagement with voicebots. In this paper, we find that users’ engagement with voicebots may be enhanced by endowing these tools with non-standard accents that deviate from “standard” pronunciation. Across a range of accents, languages, genders, and contexts, our data suggest that voicebots communicating with non-standard accents make the concept of human diversity salient in the users’ minds. As a result, voicebots communicating with non-standard accents are more readily anthropomorphized. This effect translates into greater preference for the non-standard accented voicebot in customer service settings, stronger support for startups leveraging accented vs. unaccented voicebots, higher willingness to pay for monthly subscriptions, and a greater likelihood of opting in to receive future updates and communications. Consistent with our theory, however, these effects do not hold when the anthropomorphism effect is either overridden by other cues or is undesirable for the consumer. Together, this work highlights the benefits of accented speech in improving human-AI interactions. We also hope that it sparks further investigation into factors that make technology more readily accepted by consumers.

The Pink Tax: Price Discrimination, Product Differentiation, and Gender-Based Pricing in Consumer Packaged Goods
Rong Zhang & Yu Yvette Zhang
Southern Economic Journal, forthcoming

Abstract:
This paper examines the economic mechanisms underlying persistent price gaps between products marketed to women and men, which is often referred to as the “Pink Tax.” Using NielsenIQ scanner data on toothbrushes, we provide evidence of gendered price differentials and analyze two mechanisms central to the literature: gender-based price discrimination and product differentiation. We first test for price discrimination by estimating own-price elasticities and exploiting a natural experiment created by New York State's 2020 legislation banning gender-based pricing. Our results show that women's products face significantly lower demand elasticities, and the policy intervention reduced but did not eliminate price gaps, consistent with price discrimination literature. We then estimate a structural model to recover marginal costs and markups. The results reveal that women's products are differentiated in ways that reduce substitution pressure, leading to higher markups despite lower marginal costs, which indicates that product differentiation sustains the persistent price disparities. Taken together, our findings show that price discrimination and product differentiation jointly determine gender-based pricing outcomes and that regulatory efforts aimed at banning gender-based price discrimination alone may have limited effectiveness when firms also rely on product differentiation to sustain markups.

The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
Holly Dykstra, Shibeal O’ Flaherty & Ashley Whillans
Management Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation (N = 27,227), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal.

Time-Duration Asymmetries in Consumer Decision-Making
Jiabi Wang⁠ & Kristin Donnelly
Journal of Consumer Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Consumers routinely make decisions about short time periods, such as waiting for a table or deciding whether to pay for faster delivery. Such periods are often expressed by either a duration or a clock time (e.g., if it is 6:00 PM now, “Your table will be ready in 30 minutes” vs. “Your table will be ready at 6:30 PM”). Eight experiments (N = 16,604) show that these logically equivalent frames change how long a period feels, with downstream consequences for consumer decisions. Relatively short time periods feel longer when framed by duration rather than by start and end time (i.e., clock times or calendar dates), but this pattern reverses as periods get longer. We refer to this phenomenon as time-duration asymmetry: framing an interval by its start and end time versus its duration changes how long it feels, with the direction of the effect depending on the interval’s length. We propose that this occurs because duration frames evoke compressive scalar representations shaped by diminishing sensitivity, whereas start-end frames situate time within structured categorical systems that attenuate compression. This research offers a unified framework for understanding how subtle differences in temporal framing shape perceptions of time and subsequent decisions.

Turning Uncertainty into Opportunity: Preference Uncertainty Can Be Beneficial When Consumers Have Outcome Uncertainty
Xiang Wang, Amin Shiri & Chris Janiszewski
Journal of Consumer Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Consumers can experience two types of uncertainty when purchasing a product. Preference uncertainty refers to the uncertainty associated with the horizontal product benefits one desires (e.g., “How strong do I want my coffee to be?”). Outcome uncertainty refers to the uncertainty associated with the actual benefits the product will deliver (e.g., “How strong will the coffee be?”). Ideally, retailers should strive for outcome certainty (i.e., standardize the strength profile of their coffee [coffees in their line]), and help consumers achieve preference certainty (i.e., help consumers learn their ideal coffee strength), so that consumers can purchase the appropriate product with confidence (i.e., achieve a preference-outcome match). Yet there are situations where high outcome uncertainty is a characteristic of the product class, after controlling for quality (e.g., flavor profile of wine). When outcome uncertainty is high, we paradoxically find that high preference uncertainty leads to more purchase intent than low preference uncertainty. We show this occurs because people are more optimistic that they will maximize their utility when preference uncertainty is high (i.e., multiple outcomes could potentially be the best match for their preference) than low (i.e., only one outcome could be the best match for their preference).

item.title: Teach Me — Schools and Learning
item.description:
Early Grade Retention Harms Adult Earnings
Jiee Zhong
American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, October 2026, Pages 276-308

Abstract:
This paper provides new causal evidence on the effects of grade retention on educational attainment, behavioral outcomes, and labor market performance by analyzing Texas's reading test–based retention policy. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, I find that third-grade retention significantly reduces annual earnings at age 26 by $3,477 (19 percent). While temporarily improving test scores, retention increases absenteeism, violent behavior, and juvenile crime, and reduces the likelihood of high school graduation. Moreover, retained students exhibit higher community college enrollment but lower public university attendance, though neither estimate is statistically significant.

Microdelays disrupt online learning
Asaf Mazar et al.
Nature Human Behaviour, forthcoming

Abstract:
An ever-growing share of education happens on screens. We examine an overlooked feature of modern education: ‘microdelays’ -- brief loading lags that could hinder learners with slower internet connections. In two longitudinal quasi-experimental field studies, microdelays as short as 1–2 s predicted impaired learner engagement and achievement. When faced with microdelays, US primary and secondary school students (N = 26,707) completed fewer online math assignments, took longer to complete assignments, were more likely to get distracted mid-task and earned lower scores. Likewise, when aspiring coders, primarily in Latin America (N = 55,184), experienced microdelays, they spent less time actively engaged, multitasked more often, completed fewer lessons and were less likely to attain a key course milestone. Our results held across a range of model specifications, and leverage within-person variation in load times to support a causal interpretation. These findings identify microdelays as a hitherto-overlooked barrier in online learning.

The Effect of Teacher Experience on Student Test and Non-Test Outcomes: Implications for Educational Policy
Jeongim Jin, Stephen West & Geoffrey Borman
Educational Policy, forthcoming

Abstract:
This study examined the relationship between teacher experience and multiple student outcomes in grades 4 to 6 elementary schools in a large mid-high poverty district. Outcomes considered included standardized state assessments of English language arts and mathematics, social-emotional learning, disciplinary incident count, and disciplinary incident severity. Using multilevel modeling, which adjusted for an extensive set of student and classroom composition covariates, no significant relationship was found between years of teaching and any of the student outcomes. At the student level, state test scores were associated with the student’s prior year test score, giftedness, home language, and English learner status; social-emotional and disciplinary outcomes were associated with race/ethnicity, gender, and special education status. At the classroom composition level, the mean level of the students in the classroom prior year score on the outcome variable was the key predictor of student outcomes. These findings highlight that student factors and classroom composition factors are more predictive of both academic and non-academic student outcomes than teacher experience.

Null Effects of an Intensive Teacher Leadership and Coaching Program at Scale
Michelle Doughty, Mimi Engel & Allison Atteberry
Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, forthcoming

Abstract:
Teacher coaching programs have shown promising effects on student achievement, but these effects vary substantially across programs and seem susceptible to scaling problems. Additionally, the effect of coaching on teacher retention is not known. In this paper, we evaluate a program in which current teachers are released from the classroom part-time to coach and evaluate other teachers. This program was rolled out in five cohorts of schools and eventually reached over 6,000 mentee teachers, presenting a unique opportunity to study the effect of large-scale coaching on teachers and students. We use a difference-in-differences approach with modified estimators to account for the staggered roll-out and find no effects on teacher retention or student test scores.

Jo King
Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, forthcoming

Abstract:
Suspension bans have become a popular policy response to address excessive and inequitable use of suspension in schools. However, there is little research that examines what strategies school staff employ when suspension is no longer permitted. I examine the effect of New York City’s suspension ban on the use of a potential unintended substitute for suspension: special education classification. I find that the ban induced an increase in disability classifications, especially those with higher social stigma. I show that, on average, students with these classifications experienced large declines in test scores.

item.title: Higher Power — Religion and Society
item.description:
Residual authoritarianism: Religious dones report the highest levels of left-wing authoritarianism
Daryl Van Tongeren & Shauna Bowes
Psychology of Religion and Spirituality, forthcoming

Abstract:

Religion has been linked with authoritarianism. Although most work has examined religion and right-wing authoritarianism, less work has explored the role of religion in left-wing authoritarianism (LWA). Following the religious residue hypothesis, this preregistered study examined whether residual authoritarianism may be expressed in LWA among those who left religion (i.e., religious dones). Participants (N = 804) completed measures of right-wing authoritarianism and LWA. Currently religious individuals reported the highest levels of right-wing authoritarianism, whereas formerly religious individuals (i.e., religious dones) reported the highest levels of LWA. These results suggest that after leaving religion, authoritarianism remains strong, but its orientation shifts from a right-wing to left-wing expression. Implications for the nuances of religious residue are discussed.

Parental Response to Fetal Shocks and Macroeconomic Volatility
Rakesh Banerjee & Farhan Majid
Review of Economics and Statistics, forthcoming

Abstract:

We examine parental response to a fetal shock using data from 150 Demographic and Health Surveys in 50 developing countries. Focusing on the impact of Ramadan fasting, a common shock experienced by more than a billion Muslims worldwide, we find that children exposed to Ramadan fasting during pregnancy have lower rates of full vaccination for DPT and polio compared to their non-exposed siblings. Further, parents tend to compensate for the fetal shock during booms and reinforce during economic downturns. Our estimations suggest that this has resulted in approximately half a million excess infant deaths over the past three decades.

Belief in the Real Presence Among American Catholics: Prevalence and Patterns
Brad Vermurlen, Mark Regnerus & Anne Morse
Sociological Inquiry, September 2026 

Abstract:

Pew's 2019 poll finding that only three-in-ten American Catholics affirm the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist sparked discussion and concern and was a key motivation for the 3-year National Eucharistic Revival. Using data from a nationally representative 2025 sample of Catholic adults in the United States (N = 1032) and a revised survey item measuring Eucharistic belief, this study provides an updated national estimate of belief in the Real Presence among Catholics. Our estimate is statistically indistinguishable from Pew's 2019 estimate. Moreover, we used logistic regression to identify which demographic, socioeconomic, political, and religious characteristics were most strongly associated with affirming the Real Presence. Frequency of religious service attendance and subjective importance of religious faith were the strongest predictors, whereas most demographic, socioeconomic, regional, and political characteristics mattered little. These findings reveal that belief in the Real Presence among Catholics remains at approximately three-in-ten despite significant catechetical efforts by the Church, and that variation in Eucharistic belief is associated primarily with differences in religious commitment rather than demographics or social location.

Easing the Burden? Religiosity and Educational Inequality in Pain Interference
Laura Upenieks & Markus Schafer
Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion, forthcoming 

Abstract:

A consistent inverse gradient in pain prevalence is typically observed across educational strata. Religion stands out as a source of social and personal support that may moderate the amount of chronic pain interference but may do so differently across the educational spectrum. We test competing hypotheses: The deprivation compensation hypothesis suggests that those suffering from chronic pain with lower education will benefit more from religion, whereas the enhanced resources hypothesis posits that college-educated will receive more benefit. Drawing on Wave 3 of the MIDUS study, we find that among those with chronic pain (N = 1009), respondents with less than a high school degree had the highest chronic pain interference, followed by the high school/General Education Development (GED), some college, or vocational group. Our findings suggest support for the deprivation compensation hypothesis, with religious support and coping displaying a stronger buffering association on pain interference for less educated Americans.

The Universe’s Fine-Tuning Does Call for Explanation
Roberto Fumagalli
Journal for General Philosophy of Science, September 2026, Pages 417-437

Abstract:

In recent years, several prominent authors have criticized fine-tuning arguments for failing to show that the universe’s purported fine-tuning for intelligent life calls for explanation. In this paper, I provide a systematic categorization and a detailed evaluation of the proffered critiques. I argue that these critiques cast doubt on various instances of fine-tuning reasoning, but fail to undermine fine-tuning arguments’ conclusion that the universe’s purported fine-tuning for intelligent life calls for explanation. I then explicate the implications of this result for the ongoing philosophical debate concerning the merits of fine-tuning arguments and the conditions under which specific events or states of affairs are justifiably taken to call for explanation.

Religious Cross-Pressures and Electoral Decision Making
Yara Sleiman
British Journal of Political Science, September 2026 

Abstract:

For many Americans, religious teachings are central to political identity, yet these teachings often do not align neatly with party platforms. How do voters decide when their faith crosses partisan lines? I examine this question by focusing on Catholic and Muslim Americans, whose moral and social world-views span both sides of the partisan divide. Using a novel ‘dynamic’ choice experiment, I show that religious cross-pressures shape how voters arrive at their choices. Contrary to classic accounts linking cross-pressures to disengagement, I find no evidence of increased decision avoidance; instead, voters remain engaged but simplify their choices. Cross-pressure salience is linked to greater decision difficulty, reduced information search, and greater reliance on issue prioritisation. These findings challenge the view that attitudinal conflict improves the quality of democratic participation, suggesting instead that cross-pressures constrain deliberation and may weaken the representational signal voters send to parties.

Losing Their Religion
Richard Murphy & Shqiponja Telhaj
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:

This paper studies whether governments can change social norms that constrain women’s education and work, and through which mechanism. Albania’s 1967 religion ban, which created the world’s first atheist state, provides an extreme natural experiment: religious practice was outlawed nationwide, but a 1948 classification of historic monuments determined which religious buildings remained standing. We find larger increases in female employment and schooling where no monument survived. The public visibility of the old religious order appears to be the mechanism: effects are largest where no monument remained, smaller with rural-only monuments, and smallest with urban monuments; they also decline as monument count rises, regardless of denomination. We establish how social norms can outlive formal authority.

item.title: Leadership Tenure — Regimes and Rule
item.description:
American Democracy Promotion and the Missionaries of Empire
Jeremy Menchik
Security Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
While the field of religion and international relations has grown and deepened over the past forty years, this article suggests that scholars have neglected the ways in which religious practices and structural relations shape seemingly secular policies such as democracy promotion. Security scholars have long lamented the adverse effects of democracy promotion, while comprehensive empirical reviews of democracy promotion affirm that it did not increase the likelihood of democratization. If democracy promotion did not spread democracy, what did it do? What was democracy promotion? Drawing on original interviews, research in multiple archives, and a new dataset of grants by the National Endowment for Democracy, the article demonstrates that American democracy promoters were to contemporary American liberal imperialism as Christian missionaries were to European imperialism. Democracy promotion was the ideological component of American liberal imperialism, with democracy promoters playing an analogous role to missionaries seeking to structure the social order. Key practices include universalizing a particular tradition, being sustained by mission rather than outcome, and evangelizing to sustain belief in the home church. In its claims of universality, its use of ideology as a double mask for hegemony, and its deployment of secularized theology, democracy promotion provided the motivation and legitimation for American liberal imperialism. Understanding democracy promotion as the missionary component of American liberal imperialism helps to explain aspects of the policy that were otherwise inexplicable. More theoretically, understanding democracy promotion as the missionary component of American liberal imperialism opens new avenues for scholarship on religion, empire, and international affairs.

The Victory Trap: Endogenous Opposition Coalition Weaknesses in Reversing Autocracy
Elvin Ong & Frances Cayton
Perspectives on Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
After opposition parties and alliances defeat dominant autocratic incumbents, what challenges do they encounter in reversing autocracy and what are the consequences? We argue that long-neglected endogenous weaknesses in opposition coalitions undermine re-democratization efforts, easily opening the door to autocratic comebacks. First, coalition intra-elite conflicts post-victory result in fractured and ineffective governance, generating mass disappointment with the new political elites. Second, coalition intra-supporter divergence pressures the new coalition government into implementing pro-democratic reforms at haphazard speeds and fluctuating scopes. Swift actions in reversing autocracy alienate supporters of the ex-autocrat, elicit accusations of partisan revenge, and fuel counter-mobilization against the new government. A most-different case comparison between the recent autocratic reversal experiences of Poland and Malaysia demonstrates our argument. We show in both cases that ideological and distributional conflicts among diverse coalition elites undermined governance after victory, and different supporter bases prioritized different policy agendas. Counter-mobilization by the autocratic ex-incumbents was highly successful in undermining public support for the new government. These findings suggest that profound challenges in reversing autocracy and rebuilding democracy lie within opposition coalitions themselves, in addition to authoritarian legacies.

One Message, Multiple Functions: Local Propaganda as Bureaucratic Trace Management
Jianjun Yu
Perspectives on Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
This article explores how local government propaganda in China can function as a tool for bureaucratic management. I argue that certain propaganda primarily serves as public documentation of government activities and officials’ performance, enhancing bureaucratic transparency and credibility. This documentation is particularly important when leaders lack personal ties with subordinates and thus require independent verification of their work. However, prioritizing record keeping over public persuasion often produces rigid, unengaging media content, which I term “trace-management propaganda.” Analyzing 1.4 million WeChat posts from Chinese local governments, I demonstrate that trace-management propaganda significantly increases during official evaluation periods and is especially prevalent where personal connections between leaders and subordinates are weak. A difference-in-differences analysis further confirms that a lack of personal ties increases reliance on trace-management propaganda. These findings reveal that local government propaganda in China frequently fulfills both administrative and expressive purposes, providing new insights into state media dynamics and bureaucratic oversight.

Shishir Shakya, Joshua Ammons & Towhid Iqram Mahmood
Kyklos, forthcoming

Abstract:
Using data from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project and the NAVCO catalog (1950–2019), we estimate the developmental effects of successful revolutions through difference-in-differences models and event studies. Our findings differ from common expectations: neither violent nor nonviolent revolutions consistently deliver expected development benefits. Educational indicators remain largely unchanged across both types of revolutions, and both violent and nonviolent movements are associated with lower GDP per capita. Baseline effects on life expectancy are not distinguishable from zero, though some dynamic specifications suggest positive effects for nonviolent revolutions. Our results show that while revolutions may secure political and social gains, the economic costs are large, which raises questions about whether the benefits of revolution justify these development costs.

Constitutional Political Economy, December 2026, Pages 588-619

Abstract:
Left-leaning populist regimes in 21st-century Latin America have become notoriously long, including some that maintained their power by repealing term limits. Along with changes in external factors, we argue that repealing term limits allowed populist leaders to develop longer time horizons and behave more like stationary than roving bandits. We show that, relative to those constrained by time limits, unconstrained populist leaders mitigate the economic effects of the populist cycle of boom, stagnation, and bust. Populists constrained by term limits act like roving bandits, engaging in more extractive rent-seeking that leads to more significant economic fluctuations.

Roya Izadi
Journal of Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
As international conflicts escalate, states are increasingly turning to conscription and broader public participation in national defense. This article leverages original survey data from Iran, collected before and after the unprecedented April 13, 2024 missile exchange with Israel, to show that the external threat significantly shifted public attitudes toward military service. Using matching techniques to compare responses across the two periods, I find that individuals who were surveyed after the attack were significantly more likely to support mandatory male conscription and women’s military service. Importantly, support rose despite the widespread unpopularity of conscription and Iran’s gender hierarchies. These findings demonstrate that external threats can legitimize coercion in contexts of regime distrust and reconfigure gender boundaries around military participation. The study contributes to research on public perceptions of war, coercion, authoritarian legitimacy and durability, and militarization by highlighting how external threats recalibrate the boundaries of both state authority and gendered citizenship.

Shenghua Lu & Hui Wang
Political Behavior, forthcoming

Abstract:
In the face of property rights violation, why are some groups of people more likely to take collective actions than others? In this paper, we propose that culture is an important but not fully investigated factor accounting for this question. American Democracy Promotion and the Missionaries of Empire
Jeremy Menchik
Security Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
While the field of religion and international relations has grown and deepened over the past forty years, this article suggests that scholars have neglected the ways in which religious practices and structural relations shape seemingly secular policies such as democracy promotion. Security scholars have long lamented the adverse effects of democracy promotion, while comprehensive empirical reviews of democracy promotion affirm that it did not increase the likelihood of democratization. If democracy promotion did not spread democracy, what did it do? What was democracy promotion? Drawing on original interviews, research in multiple archives, and a new dataset of grants by the National Endowment for Democracy, the article demonstrates that American democracy promoters were to contemporary American liberal imperialism as Christian missionaries were to European imperialism. Democracy promotion was the ideological component of American liberal imperialism, with democracy promoters playing an analogous role to missionaries seeking to structure the social order. Key practices include universalizing a particular tradition, being sustained by mission rather than outcome, and evangelizing to sustain belief in the home church. In its claims of universality, its use of ideology as a double mask for hegemony, and its deployment of secularized theology, democracy promotion provided the motivation and legitimation for American liberal imperialism. Understanding democracy promotion as the missionary component of American liberal imperialism helps to explain aspects of the policy that were otherwise inexplicable. More theoretically, understanding democracy promotion as the missionary component of American liberal imperialism opens new avenues for scholarship on religion, empire, and international affairs.

Abstract:
After opposition parties and alliances defeat dominant autocratic incumbents, what challenges do they encounter in reversing autocracy and what are the consequences?
